title: Research Methods in Science — Design, Analysis & Reporting

subChunks.title: Research Methods in Science — Design, Analysis & Reporting

storyBeats.txt: Theodora placed a lab notebook on the table — battered, annotated, with post-it notes in five colours. "This notebook," she said, "contains three years of experiments. Of those three years, perhaps six months produced publishable results. The rest produced errors, dead ends, and lessons. That is not failure — that is science. The public sees the published paper; the notebook contains the truth."

"Research methodology is the art of asking a question in a way that nature can answer it. A poorly designed experiment gives you an answer — but not the one you were asking. The wrong control. An unblinded assessor. A sample too small to detect the effect you care about. Methodology determines whether your conclusion tracks reality or merely reflects the noise in your data."

"Science communication is not secondary. If a discovery is made but not communicated clearly, it might as well not have been made. Peer review, open access, preprints, science journalism — every step in the chain from laboratory to public understanding can amplify or distort the signal. A scientist who cannot explain their work to a non-specialist has not fully completed the scientific task."

subChunks.hookHtml: Scientific research methods encompass the full cycle of inquiry: formulating hypotheses, designing experiments, collecting and analysing data, interpreting results, and communicating findings through peer review and publication. Each stage has its own rigour and potential pitfalls. A well-designed study produces results that others can replicate; a poorly designed one produces noise masquerading as knowledge. Understanding research methodology is essential not only for doing science but for evaluating the science that others produce — a critical skill in an era of information abundance and scientific misinformation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Scientific Method — A Structured Approach

The scientific method is an iterative process: Observation → Question → Hypothesis → Prediction → Experiment → Analysis → Conclusion → Communication → Replication → Theory. In practice, it is messier than this, with backtracking, unexpected findings, and serendipitous discoveries. However, the logical structure — falsifiable hypotheses, controlled experiments, reproducible results — is what distinguishes science from other ways of knowing.

Hypothesis: A specific, testable, falsifiable prediction. "Plants grow faster with fertiliser" is too vague. "Tomato plants watered with 2g/L ammonium nitrate will have 20% greater height after 4 weeks than control plants watered with deionised water" is a testable hypothesis with measurable outcomes.

Falsifiability (Popper): A hypothesis must be capable of being shown false. "Invisible undetectable spirits influence plant growth" is not falsifiable. Science only advances through falsification — hypotheses that survive repeated attempts at falsification gain credibility; those that do not, are rejected.

Types of Scientific Study

Experimental study (RCT, laboratory experiment): Researcher manipulates an independent variable and measures the dependent variable while controlling other variables. Highest quality evidence for causation.

Observational study: No manipulation — researcher observes naturally occurring variation. Types:

  • Cohort study: Follow a group forward in time from exposure → outcome. Can establish temporal sequence (exposure precedes outcome). E.g. Framingham Heart Study (cardiovascular disease).
  • Case-control study: Start with cases (disease/outcome) and matched controls; look backwards at exposures. Efficient for rare diseases.
  • Cross-sectional study: Survey at one point in time — association only, no temporal sequence.
  • Ecological study: Group-level data — cannot infer individual-level associations (ecological fallacy).

Systematic review and meta-analysis: Synthesis of all evidence on a question. Highest level of evidence hierarchy (above single RCTs).

Confounding, Bias, and Error

Confounding variable: A variable associated with both the exposure and outcome, creating a spurious association. Control: randomisation (RCT), matching, statistical adjustment, stratification.

Selection bias: Systematic difference between those selected and not selected for a study. Examples: survivors selecting themselves into a study (survivorship bias), healthy individuals more likely to volunteer (healthy volunteer effect).

Information bias (measurement error): Systematic error in measuring exposure or outcome. Differential misclassification (if error differs between groups) can distort results in either direction; non-differential misclassification usually biases results toward the null (reduces apparent association).

Recall bias: In case-control studies, cases (with disease) may remember past exposures differently from controls — not because exposure differs but because disease makes people think harder about possible causes.

Publication bias: Positive results are more likely to be published than negative results; the published literature overestimates the magnitude of effects. Addressed by: registering trials before starting; funnel plots in meta-analyses; mandatory publication of all trial results.

Ethical Principles in Research

The Belmont Report (1979) established three core principles for human research ethics: (1) Respect for persons (autonomy): informed consent — participants must understand and voluntarily agree to participation; special protections for vulnerable populations. (2) Beneficence: maximise benefits and minimise harms to participants. (3) Justice: equitable distribution of research benefits and burdens — avoid exploiting vulnerable populations.

Declaration of Helsinki (medical research ethics): Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972) — unethical withholding of treatment — was the historical catalyst for modern research ethics frameworks. Institutional Review Boards (IRBs, UK: Research Ethics Committees) review all human research protocols.

Animal research: 3Rs framework — Replacement (use alternatives where possible), Reduction (minimise animal numbers), Refinement (minimise suffering). Covered by Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 in UK.

Scientific Literature and Communication

Peer review: Expert evaluation of a manuscript before publication. Identifies errors, requests clarification, assesses significance and validity. Types: single-blind (reviewers anonymous), double-blind (both anonymous), open peer review (all identities known). Limitations: slow, can be biased, does not prevent all errors — peer review is a filter, not a guarantee of correctness.

IMRaD structure: Standard scientific paper structure: Introduction (why?), Methods (how?), Results (what happened?), Discussion (what does it mean?). Abstract: 150–300 word summary. Structured abstract in clinical journals.

Primary vs secondary literature: Primary: original research papers, thesis, conference proceedings. Secondary: review articles, textbooks, meta-analyses (synthesise primary literature). Tertiary: encyclopaedias, popularisations.

Open access: Research freely available online. Gold OA: publisher makes article freely available (often author pays APC). Green OA: author deposits preprint in repository. Preprints (arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv): unreviewed drafts shared publicly before peer review — accelerates dissemination, especially in emergencies (COVID-19); risk: unvetted findings can be misrepresented.

Communicating uncertainty: Scientists express uncertainty through confidence intervals, error bars, probability statements, and careful language ("the data suggest" not "the data prove"). Public and media often struggle with uncertainty — interpreting "not certain" as "not worth acting on."
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why peer review doesn't guarantee a study is correct, and what replication means in science — why does a single study, even if peer-reviewed, not settle a scientific question?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A pharmaceutical company publishes a clinical trial showing their new cholesterol drug reduces cardiovascular events by 20% (relative risk reduction) compared to placebo (p = 0.03). The trial enrolled 500 patients per group over 5 years. The absolute event rates were: drug group 4% had events; placebo group 5% had events. (1) Calculate the absolute risk reduction (ARR) and the number needed to treat (NNT) — the number of patients who need to receive the drug for one additional patient to benefit. (2) The company's press release emphasises the "20% relative risk reduction." Explain why this framing is potentially misleading compared to the ARR and NNT. (3) The trial was funded by the drug company and conducted by company employees. Identify two specific concerns about potential bias and how they could be addressed in study design. (4) The trial used a surrogate endpoint (LDL cholesterol level) as a secondary measure alongside the primary cardiovascular event outcome. Explain why surrogate endpoints can be misleading in clinical trials. (5) An independent meta-analysis of 10 trials (including this one) finds a pooled relative risk reduction of 8% (p = 0.06). How should this meta-analytic result change the interpretation of the original trial?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) ARR = event rate in placebo − event rate in drug = 5% − 4% = 1%. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.01 = 100. One hundred patients must be treated for 5 years for one additional cardiovascular event to be prevented. The relative risk reduction = ARR/control event rate = 1%/5% = 20%.

(2) Misleading framing: the 20% relative risk reduction sounds dramatic but describes a change from 5% to 4% — a 1% absolute difference. The NNT of 100 means 99 patients take the drug for 5 years and receive no personal cardiovascular benefit (though they may still benefit from LDL reduction in other ways). The relative risk reduction inflates the apparent benefit without providing the baseline context. For a patient deciding whether to take a drug with potential side effects, the absolute risk information (1% benefit over 5 years) is more clinically relevant. This distinction is important for informed consent and shared decision-making. Both RRR and ARR should be reported; presenting only RRR in press releases without ARR is a well-documented form of selective presentation.

(3) Bias concerns and mitigations: (a) Sponsorship bias (industry-funded studies more likely to show positive results — Lexchin effect): mitigation — independent data monitoring committee (DMC), independent statistical analysis, pre-registered analysis plan deposited before unblinding. (b) Investigator/conflict of interest bias: company employees designing the analysis plan may — consciously or unconsciously — choose analytical decisions favouring the drug (e.g. data cut-off, handling of dropouts, secondary endpoint selection): mitigation — full pre-registration of primary and secondary endpoints and statistical analysis plan; independent academic steering committee; transparent reporting of all pre-specified outcomes, not just those that were significant. (c) Additionally: ensure double-blinding is maintained; independent adjudication of cardiovascular events by blinded outcome assessors.

(4) Surrogate endpoint limitations: A surrogate endpoint is a biological marker (e.g. LDL cholesterol, tumour shrinkage, bone density) used as a proxy for the clinical outcome of interest (e.g. cardiovascular events, survival, fracture). Surrogate endpoints can be misleading when: the surrogate is not on the causal pathway for the clinical outcome (lowers LDL but doesn't reduce clot formation — the more relevant mechanism); the drug affects the surrogate through a mechanism that doesn't translate to clinical benefit; or the drug has adverse effects through other pathways that outweigh the surrogate benefit. Historical examples: Class I antiarrhythmics (CAST trial) suppressed arrhythmias but increased mortality; torcetrapib raised HDL but increased cardiovascular death. The regulatory gold standard is hard clinical endpoints (mortality, hospitalisation, events) not surrogate markers — especially for long-term treatments.

(5) Meta-analytic re-interpretation: The meta-analysis pools 10 trials (more power than any single trial) and finds a pooled RRR of 8% with p = 0.06. This changes the interpretation substantially: (a) The pooled effect size (8%) is less than half the original trial's reported effect (20%) — suggesting the original trial's positive result may have been inflated by chance (Type I error at p = 0.03 is possible with single trials) or by the specific trial's population/context. (b) The meta-analytic result is non-significant at p = 0.06 — the evidence across all studies combined does not reach conventional significance. This does not prove no effect, but it considerably weakens confidence in the drug's benefit. (c) The original trial should now be seen as one data point that happened to be positive — it should not be given more weight than the accumulated evidence from 10 studies. The meta-analysis represents a more reliable estimate of the true effect. Clinical guideline bodies would typically require the meta-analytic evidence before recommending widespread use.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: During the COVID-19 pandemic, multiple early observational studies suggested hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) was effective against SARS-CoV-2 infection. Several countries adopted it as treatment. Subsequent large randomised controlled trials (RECOVERY, SOLIDARITY) found no benefit and possible harm. (1) Explain what specific methodological weaknesses of the early observational studies could explain their apparently positive results, when the RCTs found none. Use at least three specific sources of bias. (2) The RECOVERY trial enrolled ≈11,000 patients and found no mortality benefit (HR ≈1.0, 95% CI 0.9–1.1). A proponent of HCQ argues: "RECOVERY used too high a dose — the study doesn't disprove HCQ at lower doses." Evaluate this argument methodologically. (3) Why are RCTs generally considered stronger evidence than observational studies for establishing drug efficacy, even if the RCT is conducted in a different population than the observational studies? (4) The rapid spread of the early HCQ observational studies was amplified by preprints and social media. Evaluate the role of preprints in scientific communication — what are the benefits and risks in an emergency? (5) After the RCT evidence emerged, some clinicians and policymakers continued to use HCQ, citing the early positive studies. Explain why this represents a misunderstanding of the evidence hierarchy, and what systems could prevent inappropriate retention of ineffective treatments in clinical practice.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Methodological weaknesses of early HCQ observational studies: (a) Confounding by indication (channelling bias): physicians may have preferentially given HCQ to healthier, earlier-presenting patients (lower severity, lower risk of death) while sicker patients received other treatments or supportive care only. The 'HCQ group' was therefore systematically less ill at baseline — they would have had better outcomes regardless of HCQ. Without randomisation, this cannot be controlled for. (b) Survival bias and time-varying confounding: patients who received HCQ early and survived to day 3 were more likely to continue HCQ and be counted as 'HCQ recipients'; patients who died within hours of starting any drug may have been excluded or categorised differently. This immortal time bias inflates the apparent benefit. (c) Lack of blinding: clinicians knowing patients were receiving HCQ may have been more attentive to those patients, provided better supportive care, or assessed outcomes differently. The Hawthorne effect — patients knowing they received a treatment — may also have affected reporting of symptoms. (d) Small sample sizes and multiple testing: many early studies had n <100; with small samples, random variation produces extreme results (either direction); positive results were published, negative were not (publication bias). (e) Unclear or inconsistent outcome definitions across studies: some measured viral clearance (surrogate), others hospitalisation, others mortality — pooling different outcomes as if equivalent.

(2) Evaluating the 'wrong dose' argument: The argument is methodologically legitimate as a hypothesis — the RECOVERY trial used a specific dosing regimen, and a different dose might theoretically have different efficacy or toxicity. However: (a) Pre-specification: the dose used in RECOVERY was based on pharmacokinetic modelling and was within ranges used in observational studies that showed benefit. If dose was the crucial variable, this should have been pre-specified as a hypothesis before the trial, not raised post-hoc after seeing negative results — this is HARKing in reverse (post-hoc criticism of methods after an unwelcome result). (b) Dose-ranging studies: the appropriate response to a dose concern is a new RCT testing alternative doses — not rejecting the existing large high-quality RCT based on untested speculation. (c) The burden of proof shifts: after a large well-powered RCT finds no benefit, the evidence strongly suggests no clinically meaningful effect; claiming a specific unstested dose would work requires positive evidence, not just identifying a possible limitation of the negative trial. (d) Biological plausibility: if the mechanism requires a specific dose window, this should be shown mechanistically before conducting another trial. The argument is potentially valid but insufficient to override a well-designed RCT without new evidence.

(3) Why RCTs are stronger than observational studies for drug efficacy: The fundamental advantage is randomisation. Randomisation distributes both known and unknown confounders equally between groups — the HCQ observational studies were affected by numerous unmeasured confounders (disease severity, comorbidities, physician preferences, timing of presentation) that randomisation eliminates by design. Even if the RCT is in a different population: the internal validity of an RCT (the confidence that any difference found is caused by the treatment) is much higher because confounding is controlled. The external validity (generalisability) is always a concern — a trial in hospitalised adults may not apply to ambulatory patients — but internal validity is the foundation. An observational study with perfect external validity but poor internal validity (confounded) tells you less about causation than an RCT with narrower external validity. This is why the evidence hierarchy places RCTs above observational studies for questions of treatment efficacy.

(4) Role of preprints in emergency science communication: Benefits: (a) Speed — preprints available within days of study completion, vs months for peer review; critical during pandemic when real-time evidence is needed for urgent policy decisions. (b) Transparency — full methods and data available for independent scrutiny immediately. (c) Community peer review — rapid informal critique by global scientific community through social media and comment systems. Risks: (a) No formal peer review — errors, methodological flaws, and inappropriate conclusions not filtered before public release. (b) Media reporting of preprints as if peer-reviewed — journalists and public cannot easily distinguish a preprint from a published paper. (c) Social media amplification of flawed preprints before they are corrected/retracted — the HCQ preprint by Mehra et al. (later retracted from The Lancet after concerns about data integrity) is an example. (d) Policy enacted on unreviewed evidence: some early HCQ recommendations were based on preprints that did not survive scrutiny. Conclusion: preprints are valuable tools that require better public communication of their provisional status and stronger media science literacy — the problem is not preprints themselves but the lack of context provided when they circulate publicly.

(5) Evidence hierarchy misunderstanding and systems fixes: The evidence hierarchy — systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs > individual RCTs > observational studies > case reports — exists because study design determines the reliability of causal inference. Continuing to cite early positive observational studies after large well-powered RCTs show no benefit represents: (a) Failure to apply the evidence hierarchy — early positive observational results are preliminary and should be superseded by stronger evidence. (b) Confirmation bias — preferentially attending to evidence that confirms prior belief. (c) Sunk cost reasoning — decisions/policies already implemented based on early evidence feel difficult to reverse. Systems to prevent inappropriate retention: (a) Adaptive clinical practice guidelines: evidence-based guidelines updated regularly by independent bodies (NICE, WHO, Cochrane) that explicitly supersede earlier guidance when stronger evidence emerges; clinicians are trained to follow updated guidelines. (b) Mandatory adverse event reporting and post-market surveillance: if a drug shows no benefit in trials but continues to be used, real-world data quickly reveal harms without benefits. (c) Medical education: training clinicians in critical appraisal — reading primary literature, understanding study design limitations, applying evidence hierarchy. (d) Regulatory frameworks: agencies (FDA, EMA) can revoke emergency use authorisations based on updated evidence; prescribing is then limited to trial contexts. (e) Open data mandates: requiring drug companies and researchers to share all trial data allows independent reanalysis and faster detection of errors or missing data.
learningObjectives: Distinguish experimental from observational study designs and explain why randomised controlled trials provide stronger evidence for causation than observational studies.
Identify confounding, selection bias, recall bias, and publication bias in described studies, and propose methods to reduce each.
Explain the ethical principles governing human and animal research (Belmont Report, 3Rs) and describe the peer review process and its limitations.
Distinguish absolute risk reduction (ARR) from relative risk reduction (RRR), calculate NNT, and explain why surrogate endpoints can mislead clinical decisions.
commonMistakes: Treating peer-reviewed publications as definitively correct — peer review filters for obvious errors and assesses plausibility, but does not prevent publication of incorrect findings; only replication across multiple independent studies builds strong scientific consensus.

Confusing relative and absolute risk — a 50% relative risk reduction sounds dramatic but may represent a change from 2% to 1% absolute risk (NNT = 100); always consider both RRR and ARR together, and the baseline risk, when evaluating clinical significance.

Dismissing a study because it was industry-funded — funding source is a risk factor for bias, not proof of bias; the appropriate response is to scrutinise the methods, pre-registration, and raw data rather than accepting or rejecting based on funding alone.

Thinking a single randomised trial settles a scientific question — individual trials, even large ones, can be Type I errors; the scientific consensus is built from multiple independent replications; systematic reviews and meta-analyses provide the most reliable aggregate estimate.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly distinguishes RCT, cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional study designs and explains the trade-offs in terms of evidence quality and feasibility.
Identifies at least three specific sources of bias in a described study and proposes appropriate methodological corrections for each.
Calculates ARR and NNT correctly from presented data, and critically evaluates the use of relative risk reduction in research reporting.
Explains peer review, open access, and preprints, identifying the advantages and limitations of each in the context of scientific communication.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Nine criteria (1965) for assessing whether an observed association is likely causal: strength of association, consistency (replication), specificity, temporality (exposure precedes outcome), biological gradient (dose-response), plausibility, coherence with known biology, experimental evidence (animal or intervention studies), analogy. No single criterion is necessary or sufficient — they are used together to build a cumulative causal argument. The criteria were originally used to establish that smoking causes lung cancer and remain the standard framework for causal inference in epidemiology.

A systematic review follows a pre-specified, rigorous protocol to identify, evaluate, and synthesise all available evidence on a question. The Cochrane Collaboration (founded 1993) produces the gold standard systematic reviews in healthcare, with rigorous methodology and regular updates. Cochrane reviews include meta-analyses where appropriate. The Cochrane Library is freely available globally. Systematic reviews are the foundation of evidence-based medicine and public health policy — NICE guidelines, WHO guidance, and clinical practice guidelines are built on systematic review evidence.

A clinical trial involving a single patient as their own control — multiple treatment periods are randomly ordered (drug vs placebo), and outcomes are measured repeatedly. Useful when: group trials are infeasible (rare conditions), individual response is more important than population-average effect, or to determine optimal individual treatment. N-of-1 trials can be aggregated across patients using Bayesian methods. They represent a shift toward personalised medicine — recognising that average effects in populations may not apply to individual patients.

A publishing format in which peer review occurs at the stage of study design (hypothesis + methods), before data are collected. If accepted (in-principle acceptance), the journal commits to publish the results regardless of outcome. This eliminates publication bias, HARKing, and p-hacking — authors cannot change their analysis plan after seeing the data. Registered Reports are now available in >300 journals across disciplines and are considered a major structural solution to the replication crisis. Results published as Registered Reports have higher replication rates than standard publications.

A clinical practice framework (Sackett, Guyatt, Evidence-Based Medicine Working Group — 1990s) integrating the best available external research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values. The hierarchy of evidence (systematic reviews > RCTs > observational studies > case reports) guides how strongly evidence should inform decisions. EBM explicitly acknowledges that not all questions can be answered by RCTs and that individual patient context (comorbidities, values, circumstances) must modify the application of population-level evidence.

questions.questionHtml: A study finds that people who drink more coffee have lower rates of Parkinson's disease (cohort study, p = 0.001, n = 50,000). A headline reads: 'Coffee prevents Parkinson's Disease — drink up!' What type of study is this, and what is the most important limitation of this conclusion?
options: An RCT — this is the strongest type of evidence and the conclusion is justified

A cohort study — the association is statistically strong but cannot establish causation; coffee drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in many ways (confounders: diet, lifestyle, genetics) that explain the lower Parkinson's rate; an RCT randomising people to coffee vs no coffee would be needed to establish causation
A case-control study — the association could be due to recall bias where Parkinson's patients forget their coffee consumption
A cross-sectional study — this design can only show correlation at a single time point and is the weakest observational design
questions.correctAnswer: A cohort study — the association is statistically strong but cannot establish causation; coffee drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in many ways (confounders: diet, lifestyle, genetics) that explain the lower Parkinson's rate; an RCT randomising people to coffee vs no coffee would be needed to establish causation
questions.explanationHtml: A cohort study follows people forward in time — coffee consumption at baseline is measured, and Parkinson's incidence is tracked over years. This establishes temporal sequence (exposure before outcome) but cannot eliminate confounding. Coffee drinkers may: exercise more (protective against PD), have different genetic backgrounds, consume better diets, have lower alcohol intake, or differ on dozens of other variables that independently affect PD risk. Even with statistical adjustment for known confounders, unmeasured confounders remain. The p = 0.001 confirms the association is unlikely due to chance — it says nothing about causation. The headline 'prevents' implies causation, which is not established. The appropriate headline: 'Coffee consumption associated with lower Parkinson's risk — cause-and-effect unproven.' An RCT randomising participants to coffee/no coffee for 20+ years would establish causation but is practically impossible. Pragmatically, converging evidence from multiple cohort studies, animal studies, and plausible mechanisms (caffeine affects adenosine receptors in dopaminergic pathways) builds a cumulative causal case even without an RCT.

questions.questionHtml: A new cancer drug is tested in a clinical trial. The control group has a 10-year survival rate of 40%; the drug group has 44%. The paper reports a 'relative risk of death' = 0.93 (p = 0.04) and calls this 'a statistically significant 7% reduction in mortality risk.' Calculate the ARR for 10-year survival and the NNT, and assess whether the conclusion is accurately framed.
options: ARR = 7%, NNT = 14; the paper is correct
ARR = 4% (44% − 40%), NNT = 25; the paper is misleadingly framing a modest absolute benefit as a large relative reduction — the 7% reduction refers to relative risk of death, not absolute risk
ARR = 0.93%, NNT = 107; the drug provides marginal benefit
ARR = 40%, NNT = 2.5; the paper understates the benefit
questions.correctAnswer: ARR = 4% (44% − 40%), NNT = 25; the paper is misleadingly framing a modest absolute benefit as a large relative reduction — the 7% reduction refers to relative risk of death, not absolute risk
questions.explanationHtml: Working through the numbers: 10-year survival: drug 44%, control 40%. 10-year mortality: drug 56%, control 60%. ARR (for mortality) = 60% − 56% = 4%. NNT (for 10-year mortality prevention) = 1/0.04 = 25. 25 patients must be treated for 10 years for 1 additional patient to survive. Relative risk of death: drug mortality/control mortality = 56%/60% = 0.933 → 6.7% relative reduction (≈7% as stated). The paper's framing: statistically accurate but potentially misleading. '7% reduction in mortality risk' — without clarification that this is relative, not absolute — sounds much more impressive than '4% absolute risk reduction.' NNT of 25 is clinically meaningful for a cancer drug (one survivor per 25 treated over 10 years), but patients deserve both the relative and absolute numbers to make informed decisions, especially given potential side effects over a 10-year treatment period. Regulatory bodies now require reporting of both RRR and ARR in drug labels.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher conducts a study, pre-registers all hypotheses, uses a double-blind RCT design with adequate sample size, finds p = 0.04 for the primary endpoint, and the paper is published in a peer-reviewed journal after rigorous review. A science journalist writes: 'This study proves the treatment works.' Is the journalist correct?
options: Yes — a double-blind RCT with pre-registration and peer review is the gold standard; the finding is proven

No — even the best-designed single RCT with p = 0.04 has a ≈5% chance of being a false positive; science does not 'prove' — it provides evidence; independent replication is needed before strong conclusions are justified, and p = 0.04 is above many modern stricter thresholds
Yes — pre-registration specifically eliminates the possibility of false positive results
No — only meta-analyses can ever prove anything; single studies are always meaningless
questions.correctAnswer: No — even the best-designed single RCT with p = 0.04 has a ≈5% chance of being a false positive; science does not 'prove' — it provides evidence; independent replication is needed before strong conclusions are justified, and p = 0.04 is above many modern stricter thresholds
questions.explanationHtml: This tests understanding of statistical inference and the philosophy of science. Even with exemplary methodology: (a) A single study with p = 0.04 has a false positive rate set by α = 0.05 — there is a ≈5% chance this result is a Type I error (rejecting H₀ when it's actually true). This probability is per test, and a single study is one test. (b) Pre-registration eliminates post-hoc hypothesis changes and p-hacking but cannot prevent the inherent sampling variability that generates false positives — it only ensures the stated probability (5%) is actually the Type I error rate. (c) Science does not 'prove' in the mathematical sense. Scientific conclusions are always provisional — open to revision with new evidence. The word 'proves' is inappropriate in scientific communication. (d) Modern statistical thinking (Benjamin et al., 2018) proposes lowering α to 0.005 for novel findings — p = 0.04 would not be significant under this criterion. (e) Independent replication by other groups in different settings is the real test of a finding's robustness. The journalist should write: 'A well-designed trial provides strong evidence that the treatment may be effective — replication studies are needed to confirm the finding.' Option D overstates — single studies are not meaningless, but individual RCT evidence is considerably strengthened by replication and meta-analysis.
